title: Kasparov’s Immortal
reviewNotes: Montages, captions and native complete diagrams reviewed. Conditional fourteen-piece mating variation only, after Black accepts Bf1 with Qxf1 at147 seconds: White Kb1/Qb2/Rb7/f3/g3/h2 against Kd1/Qf1/Rd8/Rh8/b5/f7/g6/h7. Native53 shows the complete board before the queen capture, native54 is queen animation and native55 confirms Qxf1. Native56–58 show Qc2+/Ke1/Re7+/Qe2; the final Qxe2# is a legally verified completion of the illustrated mating net. Every Black reply to the checks is enumerated: Ke1 and Qe2 are forced. This does not prove Qxf1 was forced, certify all alternatives to Bf1, or establish the actual Rd2/Rd7 game continuation and final larger queen-versus-rook conversion. Earlier full legal reconstruction and review history remain preserved.
transcript: It is not the strongest player to win the game, but the most active one. The year is 1999 and Garry Kasparov, considered by many to be the best chess player to have ever lived, is playing in a tournament against Grandmaster Veselin Topalov. And it is not too hard to see that the white pieces are much more active than the black pieces in this position. So, Garry decides to start an attack and plays knight to d4. Now, after this trade, the queen hides from the attack of the rook on d6. Topalov understands that if he can manage to get the queens off the board, the pressure on his king is going to be much lower. But this is where all hell breaks loose because Kasparov plays the incredible rook takes d4. This also defends the queen. So, if black insists on the queen trade, now this position is going to be winning for white because white has won an extra pawn. But Topalov decides to take this rook. After all, if you try to come and checkmate the black king after queen to b6, there is going to be no follow up, which is exactly why Kasparov follows up with another sacrifice, rook to e7 check. And this time if you take the rook, this is indeed going to be a checkmate, either like this or like this. But of course, black doesn't have to take the rook. He already won one of those, so he can just move the king away and be winning, right? Not exactly. Queen to d4 anyway, sacrificing the knight on a5 because now after b4, the king is forced onto a4 and it's about to get checkmated. Black has to cover b3 at all costs, but now the attack continues. Rook to a7 threatens another checkmate and the only way that black has to delay that is to sacrifice the bishop back. Of course, this rook cannot be taken because this would still be a checkmate. This gives black just enough time to play queen to d4 and try to force the queens off the board. This does give away a knight, but after all, black still has two rooks for a rook and bishop and should be better, right? Not at all. Queen takes A6 is a checkmate threat, which is why Topalov takes the A3 pawn. But after this, Kasparov doesn't stop and keeps attacking this king and pushing him further and further into the white territory. And eventually we land in this position where white is trying to find some sort of checkmate, but it seems like everything is covered by the black pieces. Kasparov needed to find some more brilliant moves here. Bishop to F1, sacrificing the bishop while attacking the black queen. But of course, if the queen takes the bishop, this is going to be a checkmate in just a few moves like this. So black plays rook to D2, and finally it seems like everything is held together, but it isn't. Rook to D7 is the final nail in this coffin. The rook is pinned to the king, so it cannot take the white queen, and this is a checkmate threat. So black takes the rook, but now the queen falls, the rook in the corner falls, and this is just a completely won end game for white, and black proceeded to resign just a couple of moves later.
